pair.title: The needle does not just point north, it tilts
pair.mini: Walk 20,000 km from the north magnetic pole to the south one. On the globe a compass needle turns right over: nose down, level, nose up. On a flat Earth with a magnet under the centre, even tuned in its favour, it stalls short: nothing past about 35° up.
pair.text: A needle free to tilt does not just point north: it dips. Along the same 20,000 km from one magnetic pole to the other, the globe turns it right over: nose down in the north, level at the magnetic equator, nose up in the south, as measured worldwide [1]. On a flat Earth with a magnet buried under the centre, with its depth set in the flat model's favour so the level circle falls on the real magnetic equator, the turn stalls: nowhere on the disc gets past about 35° up, whereas Dunedin, New Zealand, measures 72°. The red end of the needle is the north-seeking one.
pair.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: dip angles in the far south that stay shallow, as a buried central magnet predicts.
lat.title: One formula for the dip: tan I = 2 tan λ
lat.mini: On a globe with a magnet at its centre, the needle's dip I and the magnetic latitude λ obey tan I = 2 tan λ, and the field is twice as strong at the poles as at the equator. No free parameter.
lat.text: Treat the Earth as a magnet at the centre of a sphere, as Gilbert did with his terrella in 1600 [1]. The magnetic latitude λ is measured from the magnetic equator; the dip I is the angle of the needle below the local horizontal. The dipole gives tan I = 2 tan λ, and a field twice as strong at the poles as at the equator. The formula has no free parameter: once the pole is placed, every dip on Earth follows. The factor 2 makes the needle steepen fast, past 45° only 27° from the magnetic equator. The drawing is schematic.
lat.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: measured dips that depart from tan I = 2 tan λ in a way a flat layout explains.
globe.title: One magnet in the middle of a sphere
globe.mini: A single magnet at the Earth's centre. Field lines leave near the south magnetic pole, arc over, and re-enter near the north. The needle is past 45° only 27° from the magnetic equator; Paris tilts 64°.
globe.text: One magnet in the middle of a sphere, drawn at true scale. Field lines leave near the south magnetic pole, arc over the equator, and re-enter near the north one. The needle steepens fast: the factor 2 in tan I = 2 tan λ puts the dip past 45° only 27° from the magnetic equator, so the field is nearly parallel to the ground only in a narrow band; Paris already tilts 64° [1]. The real axis is tilted about 10° from the rotation axis, and a few degrees of non-dipole scatter remain [2]. The magnetic latitude shown is named above the text.
globe.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: dips that stay shallow far from the magnetic equator.
flat1.title: Flat Earth, layout 1: a magnet under the centre
flat1.mini: A magnet buried under the North Pole of a flat disc, its depth tuned so the level circle lands on the real magnetic equator. Past it the field weakens and the dip stays shallow: never past 35° up. Dunedin measures 72°.
flat1.text: The simplest flat layout: a magnet buried under the centre of the disc, its south pole facing up. Computed honestly, a vertical dipole does give a circle where the needle lies level, at √2 times its depth, and the depth is chosen here to put that circle on the real magnetic equator. Beyond it, the field dies off as 1/r³ and the dip turns shallow instead of steep: nowhere on the disc can it pass 35° up, yet Dunedin measures 72° [1]. The horizontal pull fades to about 4 μT at the rim, a fifth of what a compass in Melbourne measurably feels. The magnetic latitude shown is named above the text.
flat1.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: dips in Australia and New Zealand shallower than 35°, and a compass losing its pull toward the south.
flat2.title: Flat Earth, layout 2: a pole at the centre, the other at the rim
flat2.mini: A north pole at the centre and the south pole along the ice wall, equally strong as a magnet's poles must be. No depth puts the level circle on the real equator: Singapore gets a needle pointing down. Melbourne −9°, against −69° measured.
flat2.text: The other arrangement flat-Earth writers propose: a pole at the centre and its opposite spread along the rim, "the ice wall is the south pole". The ring is exactly as strong as the centre pole: a magnet's two poles are always equal, since field lines have no ends [3]. With equal poles no burial depth brings the level circle closer than 13,200 km from the pole, 3,200 km beyond the real magnetic equator, so the depth is fitted to ten measured dips instead. The price: Singapore and São Paulo get a needle pointing down, +13° and +9°, where it measurably points up, −16° and −40° [1]. The far south stays shallow, Melbourne −9° and Dunedin −12° against −69° and −72°, and no point on the disc passes −69°, where explorers reached a point of −90° [2]. The centre pole makes the Arctic read about 190 μT, over three times what is measured. The magnetic latitude shown is named above the text.
flat2.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: needles dipping down in Singapore and São Paulo, and near-level needles in southern Australia.
three.title: Three compasses, three predictions
three.labels: Globe|Flat: magnet under the centre|Flat: pole at the rim|Globe, field lines in 3D|Flat ①, in 3D|Flat ②, in 3D|The three needles, side by side
three.mini: The same compass under three models: a magnet at the centre of a sphere, a magnet under a flat disc, a pole spread along the disc's rim. Both flat layouts are tuned in their favour. Only the sphere matches measured dips in the south.
three.text: One compass, three models. On the globe, one magnet at the centre gives tan I = 2 tan λ: the needle turns right over from north to south, as measured [1]. Under the flat disc with a magnet buried beneath the centre, tuned so the needle lies level on the real magnetic equator, the dip never passes 35° up in the south, where Dunedin measures 72°. With a pole at the centre and an equal one along the rim, its depth fitted to measured dips, the level circle falls 3,600 km beyond the real magnetic equator, and Melbourne and Dunedin come out at −9° and −12° against −69° and −72° measured. The real dipole axis is tilted about 10° [2], which the globe carries and neither flat layout can use. The magnetic latitude shown is named above the text. Under each section, the same model in 3D, turning: its field lines are closed loops, with arrows in the direction of the field. Below, the three needles side by side at that latitude.
three.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: southern dips matching either flat layout rather than the sphere's.
dials.title: The same compass, three predictions
dials.mini: Three dip needles side by side for one observer at the magnetic latitude named above: the globe's, and those of the two flat layouts. The grey line is the local horizontal; the red end seeks north.
dials.text: Three dip circles seen edge-on, side by side, for one observer at the magnetic latitude named above the text: the globe's prediction, and those of the two flat layouts, each tuned in its own favour. The grey line is the local horizontal, north is to the right, and the red end of the needle is the north-seeking one. On the magnetic equator the globe and the first flat layout agree, because that layout was tuned there. South of it they part: the globe's needle keeps tilting up to −90°, the flat ones stall or level out. Measured values are in the International Geomagnetic Reference Field [1].
dials.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: southern dips that match one of the flat needles.
profile.title: One curve, ten cities, no free parameters left
profile.mini: Dip against distance from the north magnetic pole. The globe's dipole is a band; the flat layouts, even tuned, are two amber curves. The measured dips of ten cities ride the globe's band all the way to −90°.
profile.text: Inclination against distance from the north magnetic pole. The teal band is the globe's dipole: its width is the ±10° tilt of the magnetic axis [2], mapped through tan I = 2 tan λ; a few more degrees of non-dipole scatter are expected. The amber curves are the two flat layouts, each tuned in its favour: the first so that the needle lies level on the real magnetic equator, the second, which cannot manage that, fitted to the ten measured dips. The dots are measured values for ten cities [1], and anyone can check them against magnetic observatories [3]. The measured points ride the teal band all the way to −90° and never come near either amber curve south of the magnetic equator.
profile.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: measured southern dips lying on one of the amber curves.
needle.title: Why a compass balances differently in each hemisphere
needle.mini: The Earth's field points down at the dip angle. A compass needle on a vertical pivot can only answer to the horizontal part, so its makers counterweight it for the dip of each region. Southern compasses are balanced the other way.
needle.text: The Earth's field points into the ground at the dip angle. A compass needle on a vertical pivot is free to turn only horizontally, so it answers to the horizontal part of the field; the vertical part pulls one end down. Makers therefore counterweight needles for the dip of the region they are sold in, and a compass balanced for Europe drags in Australia, where the field points up out of the ground [1]. Manufacturers sell compasses by zone for exactly this reason. The drawing is schematic.
needle.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: one compass balance that works equally in Europe and in Australia.
dipcircle.title: The dip circle, 1581
dipcircle.mini: Robert Norman's instrument of 1581: a needle balanced on a horizontal axle at the centre of a vertical graduated circle. It reads the dip directly. Shown at 64°, roughly Paris.
dipcircle.text: A dip circle, the instrument Robert Norman, a London compass maker, described in 1581 after finding that a needle he had balanced perfectly dipped once magnetised [1]. A needle is balanced on a horizontal axle at the centre of a vertical graduated circle, and the whole is turned about a vertical stand until it lies in the magnetic meridian. It then reads the dip directly. Shown reading +64°, roughly Paris. With it, anyone can check the dip where they live against the reference field model [2].
dipcircle.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: dips read with such a circle in the south that match a flat layout.
obsbox.title: {{n}} measured sites, six models: the globe needs no tuning
obsbox.mini: Measured magnetic dip at {{n}} sites minus what each model predicts. The globe's published centred dipole sits on zero, {{gW5}} % of sites within ±5°. The best flat disc, fitted to the answers, still misses: {{fW5}} %.
obsbox.text: Each box pools one model's misses at {{n}} sites: {{src.obs.n}} magnetic observatories and {{src.survey.n}} repeat and survey stations, each with its latest measurement [1]. Observatories record around the clock and check their instruments against absolute measurements made by hand [2]. The globe's two dipoles are taken as published in the reference field model, nothing adjusted [3]: the centred one has a median miss of {{gMed}}° and {{gW5}} % of sites within ±5°; the off-centre one computed from the same model [4] sits a few degrees off. Two flat-disc layouts, calibrated so that the needle lies level on the real magnetic equator, miss by a median {{f1Med}}° and {{f2Med}}°. Fitting their free parameters to these very measurements brings the best to a median {{fMed}}°, with {{fW5}} % of sites within ±5°.
obsbox.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a flat-disc box centred on zero and as narrow as the globe's.
obslat.title: Where the misses fall: scatter for the globe, a trend for the disc
obslat.mini: Dip residual against magnetic latitude at {{n}} sites. The globe's dipole stays near zero from pole to pole. The best-fitted flat disc reads too shallow in both hemispheres: {{fN}}° north, {{fS}}° south.
obslat.text: One dot per measured site: inclination minus prediction, against magnetic latitude [1]. Top, the globe's published centred dipole with nothing fitted; bottom, a flat disc with a central pole and an equal rim ring, its burial depth fitted to these measurements. The black line joins the medians of 15° bands. The globe's line stays near zero from pole to pole; its largest misses cluster around the South Atlantic, where Earth's field departs most from a dipole [2]. The disc's line lies above zero across the north ({{fN}}°) and below it across the south ({{fS}}°): its dip does not steepen fast enough toward either pole.
obslat.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a disc residual line as flat as the globe's, with the same median north and south.
obsboxf.title: Field strength: the globe ahead on every set of sites
obsboxf.mini: Measured field strength at {{nWithF}} sites against six models. Within ±10 %: globe centred dipole {{gFw10}} %, off-centre {{eFw10}} %, fitted flat disc {{fFw10}} %. On observatories alone: {{obs.gFw10}}, {{obs.eFw10}} and {{obs.fFw10}} %.
obsboxf.text: Each box shows how far the measured total field strength at {{nWithF}} sites lies from one model's prediction, in percent [1]. The flat layouts were fitted on inclinations only and each gets a free scale factor; the globe's two dipoles keep the field strength published with the reference model, nothing adjusted [3]. Over all sites both globe dipoles do better than the fitted flat disc ({{gFw10}} % and {{eFw10}} % within ±10 %, against {{fFw10}} %), and on the {{src.obs.n}} observatories alone as well ({{obs.gFw10}} and {{obs.eFw10}} %, against {{obs.fFw10}} %). A dipole still describes the field's strength imperfectly: stronger over Asia, weaker around the South Atlantic [2]. The off-centre dipole's spread stays the narrowest in both sets. The same flat fit misses the dip by {{fN}}° north and {{fS}}° south.
obsboxf.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a flat-disc box narrower than every globe box.
field3d.title: Field lines in 3D: every loop closes
field3d.mini: The three models in 3D. On the globe, lines leave the south, enter the north and close through the Earth. Under both flat discs they close through a buried magnet. No line begins or ends anywhere.
field3d.text: The field lines of the three models, computed from the same fields as the rest of the tab and drawn in 3D, each at true scale. Arrows give the direction of the field. On the globe the lines leave the southern hemisphere, enter the northern one and close through the Earth, where the field is generated by electric currents in the liquid iron core [1]. Under the first flat layout they close through a magnet buried under the centre. Under the second they leave the rim ring, enter the centre pole and run back to the rim inside a buried disc magnetised outward. In all three, every line is a closed loop: magnetic field lines have no ends [2]. Pale lines run below the surface or inside the Earth.
field3d.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: measured field directions that follow one of the flat layouts' lines rather than the globe's dipole.
